newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Japan aid to Russia gives frayed ties belated boost.
newsitem.headline: Japan aid to Russia gives frayed ties belated boost.

text.p: Japan's decision to unblock aid to Russia will help repair ties long frayed by a bitter territorial row but the former Cold War foes are still a long way from signing a peace treaty, commentators said on Friday.
In a surprise announcement made during a visit to Tokyo by Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, Japan said it was ready to release $500 million worth of loans to Moscow.

Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda also signalled that his government would consider Russian proposals for joint development of four disputed islands that have held up the signing of a formal peace treaty since 1945.
"Today's news represents a breakthrough after so many years of poor relations," said Maxim Yusin, foreign affairs correspondent of the liberal daily Izvestiya.

The aid package, originally only for "humanitarian assistance" and restricted to medical projects, was frozen in 1991 because of political and economic turmoil in Russia following the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Loans could now be available for commercial and industrial projects, Japanese officials said on Friday.

"We are not talking about a very big sum of money but it shows that something has changed. Japan is prepared to be flexible and not to focus solely on the islands," said political analyst Viktor Kremenyuk of the USA and Canada Institute.
The tiny windswept islands of Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai group lie just off Japan's northernmost island of Hokkaido, nine time zones east of Moscow.
Seized by the Red Army in the closing days of World War Two, they have remained a stubborn outpost of Cold War tensions even after the collapse of Soviet communism.
Soviet dictator Josef Stalin forced the islands' Japanese inhabitants to leave after the war. Today they are populated by about 20,000 Russians.

Tokyo insists that Moscow return the islands, which it calls its Northern Territories. Embroiled in separate island disputes with China, Taiwan and South Korea Japan cannot afford to back down on its territorial claim for fear of a knock-on effect.

Moscow, which calls the islands the Southern Kuriles, also has limited room for manoeuvre because of strong nationalist and communist opposition in the State Duma lower house of parliament to making any territorial concessions to Russia's neighbours.
"The domination of the Duma by nationalists precludes any peace treaty because they would never agree to the territorial concessions Japan seeks," said Izvestiya's Yusin.
"The political climate remains very unfavourable to a resolution of the islands issue. It will take a long time to end this dispute," he added.

However Friday's announcement crowns a gradual rapprochement of the two sides initiated by the 1993 Tokyo Declaration in which President Boris Yeltsin recognised that a dispute existed and that it should be resolved by "law and justice".
Moscow eased visa requirements for Japanese citizens wishing to visit the islands and reduced the number of troops stationed there to around 3,500.
Joint development of the islands, if agreed by Tokyo, would probably focus on fishing, fish canneries and tourism projects.
Waters around the islands, scene of frequent clashes between Japanese fishermen and Russian coastguards, are rich in crab, salmon, and other fish.
Geologists suspect the islands are rich in minerals which have not been developed because of the row.
"The hope is that in the long run the two sides can edge towards a resolution of the islands dispute through increased contacts that help build up trust," said Kremenyuk.
Both countries have recently held elections, which means the governing teams for the next few years are probably in place, commentators noted.
But they were mindful of previous false dawns in the historically fraught relations between Russia and Japan.
"The milestone of a full peace treaty is still far off," said Kremenyuk.
